chunks: "The value is held on a capacitor, and a capacitor keeps its voltage as long as no charge can leave it.
When the sampling switch opens, the hold node is connected only to the capacitor plate, the open switch, and the input of a buffer amplifier.
If I make all of those very high impedance, the charge stays.
The buffer is the key: it's a MOSFET or JFET input amplifier with an input current of picoamps, so it can read the voltage without drawing charge.
The open switch is a MOSFET that's well off, so it leaks only a tiny reverse-junction current, typically picoamps to nanoamps.
What's left is the droop, dV over dt equals I leak over C . With 1 nanoamps of leakage on a 10 picofarad capacitor, that's 100 volts/s, or 0. 1 millivolts per microsecond.
A SAR conversion takes about a microsecond, so that's a tenth of a millivolt, well under one 12-bit LSB. But hold for 100 microseconds and you lose 10 millivolts.
So to keep it steady I use a bigger capacitor, a low-leakage switch, a low-bias buffer, short hold times, and on a board, guard rings and clean layout.
And leakage gets worse with temperature, roughly doubling every 10 degrees, so the worst case is the hot corner."
